newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Sandinistas not ready to accept defeat.
newsitem.headline: Sandinistas not ready to accept defeat.

text.p: Nicaragua's Sandinista Front will fight the results of the Oct. 20 election despite the release of the final vote count giving the apparent win to the right-wing Liberal Alliance, the Sandinista media said on Saturday.

The left-wing Sandinistas have called the vote fraudulent, and refused to accept the final results released on Friday, which gave right-winger Arnoldo Aleman an easy 51 to 37.7 percent win over Sandinista presidential candidate Daniel Ortega.
On Saturday morning the front page of the Sandinista party newspaper Barricada screamed: "God forgive them! Results Illegitimate! The Struggle Will Continue!"

Barricada's headline echoed Ortega's angry speech the night before in which he lashed out at elections officials for sanctioning the fraud, and the Catholic Church and business community for "polarizing" the election with last-minute attacks on his party before the vote.

Addressing a large Sandinista protest rally in Managua's Revolutionary Plaza, Ortega said the only way to save the "vice-ridden" elections was to call new elections in the populous departments (provinces) of Managua and Matagalpa.
"They must hold new elections in these departments, which were where the situation of total decomposition and fraudulent actions were most clearly seen," he said.
He said his party "holds the moral and political right to question these elections."

Under Nicaraguan electoral law, political parties can appeal the results of the vote count -- which the Sandinistas have said they will do -- and the Supreme Election Council (CSE) then will have eight days to rule before announcing the final winners.
While the Sandinistas said they are defending democracy, their rebellion has been criticised as a threat to Nicaragua's fledgling democracy and shaky political stability.
Nicaragua's Catholic Church, President Violeta Chamorro, the business community and international observers have all urged Ortega to accept defeat, discounting allegations of widespread fraud.
Independent of how the election council ultimately rules, the next president, due to take power on Jan. 10, will have deep wounds to heal.
But many Sandinista supporters, numerous among the unions, army and police, feel they were robbed of the elections by Liberal fraud.

"They have stolen these elections from us, and now the right-wingers will come back to oppress the people again if we don't stop them," Maria Vargas, 32, a housewife and Sandinista supporter, told Reuters.
The post-election spat has also split the Sandinista party, which, with Ortega at its head, governed Nicaragua with Soviet and Cuban backing from 1979 to 1990.
Mariano Fiallos, former CSE president and one of the most respected Sandinistas, has split from the party ranks and called for the party to accept the election results.
When asked if his party shared this opinion, a terse Sandinista commander Bayardo Arce snapped to reporters it was "the opinion of one Sandinista party member, nothing more."

While Fiallos calls for acceptance of the vote and Ortega calls for non-violent resistance, on the extreme Sandinista fringe is mayoral candidate Carlos Guadamuz who has come close to calling for a violent rebellion against the vote.
